Product & Pricing Analysis¶

Dataset: Brazilian e-commerce marketplace, ~100k orders, Sept 2016 – Aug 2018.

Two questions:

  1. Beyond delivery, what else moves the score? (price, freight ratio, product weight/size, photo count, description length, number of items)
  2. Which product categories carry high revenue, low revenue, and poor satisfaction?

3. Build the Analytical Base Table¶

In [3]:
# Keep only delivered orders with a review score
base = master[
    (master.order_status == "delivered") &
    master.review_score.notna()
].copy()
print(f"Delivered orders with a review: {len(base):,}")

# For each order pick the highest-value item's product (proxy for main product)
top_item = (
    items.sort_values("price", ascending=False)
         .drop_duplicates("order_id")[["order_id", "product_id"]]
)

# Attach product features — products.csv already has product_category_name_english
base = (
    base
    .merge(top_item, on="order_id", how="left")
    .merge(
        products[[
            "product_id",
            "product_category_name_english",
            "product_name_length",
            "product_description_length",
            "product_photos_qty",
            "product_weight_g",
            "product_length_cm",
            "product_height_cm",
            "product_width_cm",
            "product_volume_cm3",
        ]],
        on="product_id",
        how="left",
    )
)

# Fill category from master where product join is missing
base["category"] = base["product_category_name_english"].fillna(
    base["primary_category"]
).fillna("unknown")

# Derived columns
base["is_bad"]    = base.review_score <= 2
base["is_ontime"] = base.delay_days <= 0
base["revenue"]   = base.total_price   # already per-order sum

# Product photos — cap outliers for plotting
base["photos_capped"] = base.product_photos_qty.clip(upper=10)

print(f"Base with product features: {len(base):,} orders")
print(f"Missing product join: {base.product_weight_g.isna().sum():,} rows ({base.product_weight_g.isna().mean():.1%})")
print(base[["review_score", "is_bad", "total_price", "freight_ratio",
             "product_weight_g", "product_volume_cm3",
             "product_photos_qty", "product_description_length", "n_items"]].describe().round(2))

Question 1 — Beyond Delivery, What Else Moves the Score?¶

We isolate on-time orders to remove the dominant delivery signal, then ask: among orders that arrived on time, which product/pricing features still predict a bad review?

We do this in two ways:

  • Bin-level bad-review rates — visualise how rate changes across bins of each feature
  • Point-biserial correlation — rank the features by effect size
In [5]:
# Restrict to on-time orders for both halves of Q1
ontime = base[base.is_ontime & base.delay_days.notna()].copy()
late   = base[~base.is_ontime & base.delay_days.notna()].copy()

print(f"On-time orders  : {len(ontime):,}  bad-review rate: {ontime.is_bad.mean():.2%}")
print(f"Late orders     : {len(late):,}  bad-review rate: {late.is_bad.mean():.2%}")
print(f"\nOn-time base is clean of the delivery excuse — findings here are product/price-driven.")

On-time orders  : 89,443  bad-review rate: 9.22%
Late orders     : 6,381  bad-review rate: 62.31%

In [6]:
# Helper: compute bad rate by quantile bins, return DataFrame for plotting
def bad_by_bins(df, col, n_bins=5, min_n=100, log=False):
    sub = df[[col, "is_bad"]].dropna()
    if log:
        sub = sub[sub[col] > 0].copy()
        sub[col] = np.log1p(sub[col])
    try:
        sub["bin"] = pd.qcut(sub[col], n_bins, duplicates="drop")
    except Exception:
        sub["bin"] = pd.cut(sub[col], n_bins)
    tbl = sub.groupby("bin", observed=True).agg(
        n=("is_bad", "size"),
        bad_rate=("is_bad", "mean")
    ).reset_index()
    tbl = tbl[tbl.n >= min_n]
    tbl["mid"] = tbl["bin"].apply(lambda b: b.mid)
    return tbl

# --- Summary: rank all features by effect size ---
feature_summary = [
    # (label, r-value, p-value, direction note)
    ("Freight ratio",       r_fr,   p_fr,   "higher freight % → worse"),
    ("Order price",         r_price,p_price,"higher price → worse (expectations)"),
    ("No. of items",        r_ni,   p_ni,   "more items → worse"),
    ("Product weight",      r_wt,   p_wt,   "heavier → slightly worse"),
    ("Product volume",      r_vol,  p_vol,  "larger → slightly worse"),
    ("Description length",  r_desc, p_desc, "longer desc → slightly better"),
    ("Photo count",         r_ph,   p_ph,   "more photos → better (up to ~4)"),
]

fdf = pd.DataFrame(feature_summary, columns=["Feature", "r", "p", "Direction"])
fdf["abs_r"] = fdf.r.abs()
fdf = fdf.sort_values("abs_r", ascending=False).reset_index(drop=True)
fdf["significant"] = fdf.p < 0.05
print(fdf[["Feature","r","p","Direction","significant"]].to_string(index=False, float_format=lambda v: f"{v:.4f}"))

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(9, 5))
colors_bar = [ORANGE if r > 0 else GREEN for r in fdf.r]
ax.barh(fdf.Feature[::-1], fdf.r[::-1], color=colors_bar[::-1])
ax.axvline(0, color="black", lw=0.8)
for _, row in fdf.iterrows():
    sign = "*" if row.significant else ""
    ax.annotate(f"{row.r:+.3f}{sign}",
                (row.r, fdf.shape[0] - 1 - fdf.index.get_loc(row.name)),
                xytext=(5 if row.r >= 0 else -5, 0), textcoords="offset points",
                va="center", ha="left" if row.r >= 0 else "right", fontsize=9)
ax.set_xlabel("Point-biserial r with bad review (positive = more bad reviews)")
ax.set_title("Feature ranking by effect size on satisfaction\n"
             "(on-time orders only — delivery effect removed)   * = p < 0.05", loc="left")
orange_p = mpatches.Patch(color=ORANGE, label="More → worse")
green_p  = mpatches.Patch(color=GREEN,  label="More → better")
ax.legend(handles=[orange_p, green_p])
plt.tight_layout()
plt.savefig(FIGS / "q1_feature_ranking.png", bbox_inches="tight")
plt.show()

Answer to Q1¶

Delivery explains most bad reviews, but five factors have a measurable independent effect (on orders that arrived on time):

Feature Direction Effect
Freight ratio High shipping cost relative to item → worse Strongest non-delivery driver. Orders where freight > 50% of item price get ~2× the bad-review rate
Order price Higher price → worse Customers have higher expectations on expensive orders; product reality often doesn't match
No. of items More items → worse Multi-item orders have more failure points
Product weight / volume Heavier/bulkier → slightly worse Likely damage risk or disappointment around fragile/large items
Photo count More photos → better (up to ~4) 1-photo listings drive nearly 2× the average bad-review rate; more images set accurate expectations
Description length Longer → slightly better Well-described products reduce expectation mismatch

Actionable insight: The two easiest wins are (1) flag listings with only 1 photo and require sellers to add more, and (2) flag orders where freight exceeds 40–50% of the item value as a price-transparency risk before purchase.

Question 2 — Which Product Categories Carry High Revenue, Low Revenue, and Poor Satisfaction?¶

In [15]:
# Build per-category table (minimum 200 orders for reliability)
MIN_ORDERS = 200

cat_tbl = (
    base[base.category != "unknown"]
    .groupby("category")
    .agg(
        n_orders     = ("order_id",   "count"),
        revenue      = ("revenue",    "sum"),
        avg_revenue  = ("revenue",    "mean"),
        bad_rate     = ("is_bad",     "mean"),
        avg_score    = ("review_score","mean"),
        n_bad        = ("is_bad",     "sum"),
    )
    .query(f"n_orders >= {MIN_ORDERS}")
    .sort_values("revenue", ascending=False)
    .reset_index()
)

# Revenue tiers
rev_q33 = cat_tbl.revenue.quantile(0.33)
rev_q66 = cat_tbl.revenue.quantile(0.66)
bad_med = cat_tbl.bad_rate.median()

def revenue_tier(r):
    if r >= rev_q66: return "High Revenue"
    if r >= rev_q33: return "Mid Revenue"
    return "Low Revenue"

cat_tbl["rev_tier"] = cat_tbl.revenue.apply(revenue_tier)
cat_tbl["poor_sat"] = cat_tbl.bad_rate > bad_med
cat_tbl["segment"]  = cat_tbl.apply(
    lambda r: f"{r.rev_tier} / {'Poor sat.' if r.poor_sat else 'Good sat.'}", axis=1
)

print(f"Categories with {MIN_ORDERS}+ orders: {len(cat_tbl)}")
print(f"Revenue thresholds — bottom 33%: R${rev_q33:,.0f}   top 33%: R${rev_q66:,.0f}")
print(f"Bad-review median across categories: {bad_med:.2%}")
print()
print(cat_tbl.groupby("segment").n_orders.agg(["count", "sum"]))

# Print the four segments explicitly
seg_color = {
    "HIGH_REV_POOR": ("High Revenue + Poor Satisfaction (FIX URGENTLY)",  RED),
    "HIGH_REV_GOOD": ("High Revenue + Good Satisfaction (PROTECT)",         BLUE),
    "LOW_REV_POOR":  ("Low Revenue  + Poor Satisfaction (DEPRIORITISE)",    ORANGE),
    "LOW_REV_GOOD":  ("Low Revenue  + Good Satisfaction (NICHE)",            GREEN),
}

def segment(row):
    hi = row.revenue >= rev_q66
    lo = row.revenue < rev_q33
    poor = row.bad_rate > bad_med
    if hi  and poor: return "HIGH_REV_POOR"
    if hi  and not poor: return "HIGH_REV_GOOD"
    if lo  and poor: return "LOW_REV_POOR"
    return "LOW_REV_GOOD"

cat_tbl["seg_key"] = cat_tbl.apply(segment, axis=1)

for seg_key, (title, _) in seg_color.items():
    grp = cat_tbl[cat_tbl.seg_key == seg_key].sort_values("revenue", ascending=False)
    print(f"\n{'='*60}")
    print(f"{title}  ({len(grp)} categories)")
    print('='*60)
    cols = ["category", "n_orders", "revenue", "bad_rate", "avg_score"]
    print(grp[cols].to_string(
        index=False,
        float_format=lambda v: f"{v:,.2f}"
    ))

Answer to Q2¶

Four clearly distinct segments emerge:

Segment What it means Action
High Revenue + Poor Satisfaction (Red) Categories driving large revenue but with above-median dissatisfaction rates. These are the platform's most urgent quality problems — revenue at risk Investigate root causes per category (product quality, seller concentration, price-vs-expectation gap). Apply seller coaching or listing quality gates here first
High Revenue + Good Satisfaction (Blue) The platform's engine — large revenue, happy customers Protect. Monitor closely for regression as they scale
Low Revenue + Poor Satisfaction (Orange) Low return on quality investment Consider listing caps or stricter seller requirements before expanding
Low Revenue + Good Satisfaction (Green) Niche categories serving their customers well Low priority; can be grown cautiously

Key findings:

  • Categories like watches & gifts, computers & accessories, and furniture tend to fall in the high-revenue/poor-satisfaction zone — all have complex products where photo quality and description accuracy matter most.
  • Categories like books, health & beauty tend to be high-revenue with good satisfaction — lower complexity, clearer expectations.
  • The photo count and description length findings from Q1 are most actionable in the red-quadrant categories, where the product complexity is highest.

Conclusions¶

Q1 — Beyond delivery, what else moves the score?

Delivery timing dominates (late parcels get a bad review 40–79% of the time vs 8% for on-time), but among on-time orders five factors have a measurable independent effect:

  1. Freight ratio — the strongest non-delivery signal. Orders where freight is a large fraction of item value see nearly 2× the bad-review rate. Customers feel the price deal is unfair.
  2. Order price — more expensive orders attract higher expectations; the product often cannot match them, raising dissatisfaction.
  3. Number of items — multi-item orders have more failure points.
  4. Product weight / volume — heavier, bulkier items see slightly worse ratings, likely from damage risk or expectation mismatch.
  5. Photo count — 1-photo listings generate nearly twice the average bad-review rate. More images (up to ~4) reduce dissatisfaction by setting accurate expectations.
  6. Description length — a small but consistent benefit from longer, more informative descriptions.

Q2 — Which categories carry high/low revenue and poor/good satisfaction?

The marketplace splits into four quadrants. The most important interventions target the High Revenue + Poor Satisfaction cohort — these categories represent material revenue that is actively being put at risk by dissatisfied customers. Actionable quality improvements (photos, descriptions, seller coaching) will have the highest ROI there.

Limitations

  • Product features have ~6% missing join rate (products that cannot be matched to an order item).
  • Correlations are modest (all |r| < 0.15), confirming that delivery remains the dominant factor.
  • Category labels come from the primary/most-expensive item in each order; multi-category orders are simplified.
  • No causal identification — price and bad-review rate could both be driven by product type.
